source.title: The Expert Strikes Back: Interpreting Mixture-of-Experts Language Models at Expert Level
source.authors: Jeremy Herbst; Jae Hee Lee; Stefan Wermter

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether sparse MoE routing is associated with less neuron-level polysemanticity in LLMs, using k-sparse probes rather than the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper cites toy-model superposition results from other work; those cited results are not rows. The study’s own relevant results are k-sparse probing comparisons between MoE experts and dense FFNs. Exact plotted F1 values are not stated in the text. Automatic expert-labeling and trigger-target results do not directly measure the claim versions recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study's own k-sparse probing results compare how concentrated concepts are in single neurons of MoE experts versus dense FFNs across 12 production LLMs. This bears on V4 (whether real models spread features across neurons) and, through a total-parameter control, on V2 (the capacity account). The setting is new: MoE versus dense LLMs rather than toy models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MoE expert neurons are less polysemantic than dense FFN neurons, with the gap widening as routing gets sparser. They attribute this to sparse routing rather than total parameter count. They also conclude that whole experts are interpretable fine-grained task specialists. They concede that experts are not fully monosemantic and that superposition, including between experts, may remain.
record.recipe_differences: Uses k-sparse linear probes and best-layer/best-expert selection on trained LLMs, rather than the original toy-model construction and geometric measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that probe performance and interpretability vary with routing sparsity; it also selects the best layer and, for MoEs, the best expert for each concept. Exact intermediate-k values were not extracted.

fits_no_version.finding: Expert-level automatic interpretability: most experts score F1 >0.8 on LLM-generated labels, with higher scores for sparser-routing models. Trigger-target DLA shows labelled experts are top contributors on matched prompts and not routed in 80% of control prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whole MoE experts act as interpretable functional units, with interpretability increasing as routing gets sparser.

fits_no_version.finding: The JSD specialization scores show experts specialize at fine granularity (k=5000 clusters), not as broad domain specialists.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE experts are fine-grained task specialists rather than domain or token-level specialists.

record.problems: The probe results are indirect evidence about neuron-level polysemanticity, not direct measurements of feature overlap or direction geometry. Exact F1 values are shown in figures but not stated in the text. Best-layer and best-expert selection reports an upper-bound-style comparison; MoE data are filtered to tokens routed to the expert. The paper notes that the largest current MoE models, including DeepSeek-V3, were not included.
record.rows_left_out: The remaining k values in Figures 1, 3, and 8 and the routing-sparsity curves in Figure 4 are not separately extracted; exact plotted values are unavailable in the text. Expert-labeling, causal attribution, specialization-score, and taxonomy results are not rows for these claim versions. Cited toy-model results are excluded because they are not this study’s results.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, no feature-count vs dimension manipulation, no geometry or sparsity phase transition. Toy-model results are only cited (Chaudhari et al.).
Feature importance, dedicated dimensions for important features, and explicit allocation among competing features. Only total versus active parameter count is varied.
No test of non-capacity mechanisms for polysemanticity.
No SAE or dictionary recovery of sparse features; evidence is supervised single-neuron probe decodability of 58 predefined concepts.
Not tested; SAEs are not used.
Not tested; feature dimensionality is not examined.

missing.what: Best-layer F1 across k grouped by routing sparsity NA/N (0.06, 0.08, 0.12, 0.25): sparser routing gives cleaner single-neuron representations. This is the key dose-response result for whether distributed coding (V4) varies with sparsity.

Per-concept-category scatter: MoE beats dense across POS, LaTeX, code and text, with 'nearly every point' above the equality line. Also MoE has lower variance across concepts, whereas dense models fail some concepts entirely.
Number of experts per concept within 95% of the best expert's F1: whether concepts are spread across experts. This relates to the authors' own caveat about superposition between experts.

record.verdict_notes: All F1 values are figure-only (the y-axis starts at 0.80), so the size of the dense-model 'struggle' is unclear. There are two methodological asymmetries favouring MoE. First, MoE probe data are restricted to tokens routed to the expert, an easier and narrower distribution. Second, best-expert selection over 32–128 experts per layer gives more chances than a single dense layer. Either could inflate apparent monosemanticity independent of superposition. The V2 link is kept only for the OLMo total-parameter control. The sparsity trend fits a 'fewer features per unit' capacity reading, but the study does not separate this from data filtering.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test small toy networks, feature counts exceeding dimensions, near-orthogonal overlapping directions, interference, or the claimed sparsity-dependent geometric transition.

It tests the association between routing sparsity and neuron-level probe performance/polysemanticity, and compares parameter-matched models. It does not test feature importance, dedicated dimensions for important features, or an explicit allocation of dimensions among competing features.
It does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
It measures concept decodability from individual neurons with k-sparse probes in LLMs. It does not use SAEs or establish feature recovery by a dictionary.
It does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
It does not measure whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions or compare them with multidimensional features.

tranche.reason: The study tests distributed concept representation in the new setting of production MoE experts compared with dense FFNs.

source_check.notes: Exact probe F1 values are figure-only. Single-neuron recoverability on routed subsets is indirect evidence about polysemanticity; it does not establish global monosemanticity or isolate a causal effect of routing.

statements.correction: OLMoE-1B-7B outperforms OLMo-7B despite the dense model having 7× more active parameters per token. Authors attribute the difference primarily to sparse routing. Feature competition and importance-dependent capacity allocation are not measured.
statements.problem: The comparison and authors' attribution are accurately reported, but their interpretation as a limitation of V2 exceeds what the experiment tests.

statements.correction: OLMo-family comparison controls total parameter count. OLMoE shows cleaner probed representations than OLMo-7B. Routing sparsity is associated with reduced polysemanticity; routing is not independently manipulated.
statements.problem: The study supports an association across models; saying sparse routing changes selectivity implies an isolated causal manipulation.
